blocks: Penicillin makes bacteria burst, and it barely touches your own cells. Here's how.
Many bacteria wrap themselves in a wall made of a mesh called peptidoglycan. It's what keeps them from bursting.
To grow, they keep weaving new mesh, and enzymes stitch the strands together.
Penicillin jams those stitching enzymes. The wall weakens, water pushes in, and the bacterium pops.
Your cells don't make peptidoglycan at all, so the target only exists in the enemy. Viruses don't have it either. That's why antibiotics do nothing for a cold or the flu.
Alexander Fleming spotted it in nineteen twenty-eight, when a mould on one of his plates killed the bacteria around it.

But bacteria evolve. Some make enzymes that cut penicillin apart. A study in The Lancet estimated that resistant bacteria directly caused about one point two seven million deaths worldwide in twenty nineteen.
Antibiotics are prescription medicines. The standard advice: take them only when a doctor prescribes them, and exactly as prescribed.
